transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, yes, thank you. Well, I'm here because... I mean, I’m a secondary school teacher, so obviously reading and grading is a massive part of my day-to-day life. And it’s just become incredibly frustrating trying to get through my workload. I’ll set everything up perfectly, you know, I'll have my coffee, my desk is clear, I tell myself 'Okay, time to focus'—and I can sit down with a giant stack of student essays or a thick curriculum document, fully intending to just put my head down and work. 

But then, maybe ten minutes will go by, and I suddenly realize I’ve just been staring at the exact same page the entire time. My eyes are physically on the paper, but I'm just... I'm thinking about three completely different things. Like, I'll be worrying about an email I need to send to a parent, or wondering if I have enough time to run to the store later, or just replaying a conversation from the staff room. I'm barely taking in a single word of what’s right in front of me. It's just exhausting because I really want to get it done, I set the time aside, and then I just sit there lost in my own head, and it takes me hours to do something that should take maybe thirty minutes. So, yeah, that's really the main thing that drove me to make the appointment.

Do you find that this kind of difficulty with focusing happens in other parts of your life, like when you're reading a book for pleasure, having a conversation, or following through on household tasks?

Well, yeah, actually. It's funny you mention conversations, because that's... that's a big one, actually. It’s not just the reading. It happens all the time when people are talking to me, which is honestly really embarrassing. Like, at school, we have these departmental planning meetings every Tuesday afternoon. And I know they're important, we're discussing the syllabus for the next term, coordinating resources, that sort of thing. And I am sitting there, I am looking right at the head of the department, I am nodding along, making what I think is excellent eye contact, giving all the right physical cues that I am fully engaged in this professional discussion. 

But then, inevitably, someone will turn to me and say, "So, what do you think about that approach for the Year 10s?" or something like that. And my stomach just completely drops. Because I suddenly realize I haven't heard a single word they've said for the last five minutes. My brain was just... off somewhere else entirely. Maybe thinking about a lesson plan, or what I'm going to make for dinner, or just some random thought about a documentary I watched last week. And it happens at home with my wife, too, which is even worse, really, because it causes arguments. She’ll be telling me about her day, or explaining something we need to do for the house, and I’m doing the exact same thing—looking right at her, nodding, saying "uh-huh"—and then she'll ask my opinion and I just have to sit there and admit I completely missed the actual point of what she was saying. It makes me feel terrible, like I don't care, but I do care! I just... the words go in my ears but they don't stick in my brain. It's incredibly frustrating, and honestly, it makes me feel like a terrible listener, both as a husband and a colleague.
Have you ever found yourself feeling restless, fidgety, or unable to sit still for long periods of time, or do you often feel like you need to be moving or doing something?

No, not really. I mean, I know that's a thing people talk about when they talk about... well, this sort of thing, but I don't really get that physical restlessness. I'm actually pretty content to just sit. Like, I can sit at my desk for hours, physically speaking. I don't feel this overwhelming urge to get up and pace around the classroom or bounce my leg or anything like that. 

In fact, my wife always jokes that once I sit down on the sofa in the evening, I'm practically glued to it. I'll just sit there, maybe staring at the TV, or more likely just staring into space, completely lost in thought. It's almost the opposite of being hyperactive, I think? I mean, my brain is definitely going a million miles an hour, bouncing from one thought to the next, like I was saying before about the meetings and the reading. It's like my mind is running a marathon, but my body is perfectly still. 

I don't find myself needing to fiddle with pens or tap my fingers, either. Sometimes I'll doodle a bit in the margins of my notebook during those department meetings, just sort of drawing boxes or shading things in, but I think that's more of an attempt to try and anchor my attention, you know? Like if I keep my hand moving just a little bit, maybe I'll actually hear what the head of department is saying. But it's not a nervous energy or a feeling of being trapped in my chair. It's really just the mental side of things—the spacing out, the losing track of the conversation, the staring at the same paragraph for twenty minutes. Physically, I'm fine just staying put.
Have you been feeling down, sad, or hopeless most of the day, nearly every day, or have you lost interest or pleasure in most activities you used to enjoy?

No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, I definitely get frustrated, obviously, like I was saying about the grading and the meetings. It's incredibly annoying to feel like my brain is just... slipping gears all the time. But it's not sadness. I definitely don't feel hopeless. Actually, I feel pretty optimistic most days, which is why I wanted to come in and finally figure this out, you know? 

And as for losing interest in things... no, definitely not. If anything, I get really deeply invested in the things I actually enjoy. Like I mentioned those documentaries earlier—I still absolutely love watching them. Just this past weekend, I went down this massive rabbit hole watching a four-part series on the history of the London Underground, and I was completely fascinated. I spent half of Sunday telling my wife all these random facts about the excavation of the Victoria line while she was just trying to read her book on the sofa. 

And I still love cooking, I still play five-a-side football with some of the other teachers on Thursday nights... I never lose the desire to do those things. The enjoyment is absolutely still there. It's really just the execution of the mandatory, tedious stuff that gets me stuck. I don't wake up feeling like there's a dark cloud over me or a heavy weight on my chest or anything like that. It's more of a... a logistical frustration, if that makes sense? Not an emotional void. My wife would be the first to tell you I'm generally a pretty upbeat guy. I'm just, you know, a bit scattered when it comes to the things I actually *have* to do. So, yeah, definitely not sad or hopeless.
Looking back, were you already experiencing difficulties with concentration or attention before you turned 12 years old?

Oh, absolutely. Yeah, long before I was 12. I mean, if you were to go back and look at my primary school report cards—which my mum actually still has, she kept this whole box of them in her loft, bless her—it's like reading the exact same story over and over again. Every single year, it was the exact same comments from my teachers. They'd always write things like, "He's a bright boy, but he's just so careless." Or, you know, they'd put down, "Doesn't finish his work unless closely supervised." 

And they really meant *closely* supervised. Like, the teacher would literally have to stand right over my desk, practically tapping the paper, just to keep me from staring out the window at the playground or, I don't know, examining the wood grain on my desk. If they walked away to help another student, my focus would just... poof. Gone. 

And the homework... oh, the homework was an absolute nightmare for my parents. It wasn't that I couldn't understand the material, it was the actual logistics of getting it done and handed in. My mum and dad were constantly, and I mean *constantly*, finding these utterly crumpled up worksheets just shoved into the very bottom of my backpack. You know, mixed in with old biscuit wrappers and broken pencils and bits of string. I'd maybe do the worksheet—or half of it, anyway—and then I'd just shove it in my bag and completely forget it even existed, let alone remember to actually pull it out and turn it in to the teacher the next morning. 

My mum used to get so frustrated. She'd pull out this crinkled, half-torn piece of paper with maths problems on it and say, "Why didn't you hand this in? You did the work!" And I never had a good answer for her. I just... I genuinely forgot. It was like the second the paper went into the bag, it ceased to exist in my reality. So yeah, it's definitely not a new thing at all. It's been happening since I was a little kid just trying to get through Year 3 or 4. It's funny how you don't connect the dots until you're an adult, you know? But looking back, the signs were literally written down in black and white by my teachers.
